venues.d: The city's finest address — a former bank on Passeig de Gràcia, all light, calm and quiet precision.

venues.n: Hotel Arts Barcelona, A Ritz-Carlton Hotel
venues.d: The great seafront tower — 44 storeys above the beach, under Gehry's golden fish.
The city's original grande dame — opened in 1919 as the Ritz, and still Barcelona's most classical grand hotel.
A neo-Gothic Passeig de Gràcia mansion turned destination hotel — home to the city's first three-star table.
Ian Schrager's cool, low-lit house in the old town — a rooftop and a nightclub under one modern roof.

venues.n: The Cotton House Hotel, Autograph Collection
venues.d: The former Cotton Textile Foundation, reborn — a spiral staircase, a library bar and old-world tailoring throughout.
A 1911 Modernista landmark by Domènech i Montaner — the most beautiful building any Barcelona hotel occupies.
A family-owned classic on Passeig de Gràcia, one block from Gaudí's La Pedrera.
A boutique house built over a Roman wall in the Gothic Quarter — history you can touch, calm you can keep.
An intimate waterfront boutique on the site of Picasso's first studio, looking to the marina.
A sleek contemporary house on Gran Via with a rooftop pool and terrace over the city.
A design-forward house wrapped in a rippling white façade, with a rooftop pool above the Eixample.

venues.n: The One Barcelona, a Luxury Hotel
venues.d: A quietly opulent H10 flagship a street from Passeig de Gràcia, with a rooftop plunge pool.
A serene townhouse hotel around a hidden garden courtyard — a pocket of quiet off Passeig de Gràcia.
An adults-only townhouse tucked into a Gothic-Quarter lane — clubby, discreet and green-corniced.
A contemporary boutique in leafy Gràcia — away from the crowds, close to the neighbourhood's tables.
The members' club's seafront house in the old town — a rooftop pool and that familiar House ease.
A small hotel above one of Spain's great restaurants, in the green calm of the upper city.
A tall, contemporary tower with a 23rd-floor pool and 360-degree views across the city.
A French-run beach-side house opposite Hotel Arts, with rooftop pools over the Mediterranean.
The sail-shaped tower at the end of the beach — the city's most photographed modern silhouette.
A 12th-century palace on a hidden Gothic-Quarter square — candlelit, intimate, deeply romantic.
A 1920s house between the Gothic Quarter and El Born, crowned by a rooftop infinity pool.
A warm, art-filled house in the heart of the Gothic Quarter, with a rooftop bar and pool.
A quiet boutique with a garden terrace, a step from Gaudí's La Pedrera.
A polished, well-run house on a passage near El Born, with a small rooftop pool.
The larger suites of the Cotton House, for a family taking more room in one of the Eixample's most characterful houses.
The best restaurant in the world — three ex-elBulli chefs at the absolute summit of playful, avant-garde cooking.
Martín Berasategui and Paolo Casagrande's flawless haute cuisine — the first restaurant in Barcelona to hold three stars.
Jordi Cruz's ambitious, half-classic half-avant-garde tasting menu, in the green calm of the upper city.
The Torres twins cook in the middle of a vast open kitchen — theatre and three stars in an old tyre workshop.
Albert Adrià's most personal project — a shifting, dreamlike journey through a series of rooms.
Paco Pérez's sea-and-garden cooking on the seafront — two stars held for well over a decade.
A deeply personal ode to Catalan produce and memory — raised to two stars and richly deserving.
Ingredient-driven cooking inside Domènech i Montaner's Casa Fuster — gastronomy and architecture in one room.
Tapas raised to two-star technique — the most exciting small-plates room in the city.
The Ruscalleda family's refined Catalan cooking, in the calm of the Mandarin Oriental.
Jordi Cruz's more accessible room — precise, contemporary Catalan cooking without the ABaC ceremony.
Albert Raurich's Asian-Spanish tapas at a black-lacquered counter — elBulli technique, izakaya soul.
Hideki Matsuhisa's Japanese counter in the Gothic Quarter — Barcelona's benchmark for sushi and kaiseki.
Romain Fornell's classical French-Catalan cooking, and an intimate kitchen table for the curious.
A Belle Époque institution open since 1967 — grand, classical Catalan dining and a legendary cellar.
Martín Berasategui's Basque-rooted brasserie downstairs from Lasarte — refined, and a little easier to book.
The much-loved cooking school's restaurant — technically immaculate Mediterranean, and famous pastries.
An intimate room doing quietly inventive, market-led Catalan cooking — a long-held, understated star.
Jordi Vilà's temple of modern Catalan cooking, inside a Moritz brewery — tradition, reimagined.
The cooking of the Ebro delta brought to the city — rice, eel and river produce, done with real finesse.
The successor to Hoja Santa — Paco Méndez's dazzling, avant-garde Mexican cooking.
A young, personal kitchen weaving Catalan and Mexican threads — one of the city's most characterful stars.
Jordi Cruz's third city star — refined, contemporary cooking in an elegant Eixample room.
A bold newcomer built around 'charcuterie of the sea' — one of the freshest ideas in the city.
Inventive, globally-inspired cooking that earned a first star in the elegant upper city.
A precise, quietly ambitious newcomer — a first star for a kitchen worth seeking out.
A tiny, characterful room doing seasonal Mediterranean plates with Asian and South-American touches.
Chef Miquel Pardo's generous tasting menu — Castellón roots, brilliant value, always full.
A cramped, joyful Venetian kitchen hidden behind the Boqueria — cicchetti and fresh pasta done properly.
Catalan 'platillos' and monthly specials in a village-quiet corner of Sarrià, with a lovely terrace.
An easy, well-priced neighbourhood room doing careful market cooking — a local favourite for good reason.
Cooking built around 'ripeness' — local produce, a French hand, and real value in the upper city.
Dani Lechuga's meat-obsessed counter — steak tartare and cuts handled with real seriousness.
A young, spontaneous bistro with globally-inspired cooking and a wine list to match.
A poetic, plant-forward kitchen — creative, seasonal cooking with vegetables at the centre.

Gaudí's unfinished masterpiece, the tallest church in the world since the Tower of Jesus Christ topped out at 172.5m in 2026. Go early or book a late slot to see the nave's stone-forest columns lit by the stained glass — warm reds and golds in the west windows at sunset, cool blues in the east at dawn. Buy timed tower access in advance; the lift up a spire is worth the vertigo.

Gaudí's whimsical hillside garden-city, all serpentine trencadís mosaic benches, the tiled salamander, and the terrace looking straight down to the sea. Book the timed Monumental Zone entry; arrive at opening to have the colonnaded viaducts to yourself before the crowds. The surrounding free park is a lovely, shaded stroll for families.

The most theatrical house on the block — a shimmering facade of broken blue-green glass, bone-like balconies, and a dragon's-back roof. The evening tours and the immersive light-and-sound installation on the top floor are the discreet way to see it without shoulder-to-shoulder crowds.

Gaudí's rippling stone apartment block, nicknamed 'the quarry.' The real prize is the rooftop, where the chimneys stand like helmeted warriors framing the Sagrada Família. Come back after dark for 'La Pedrera Night Experience,' a rooftop show with projections — an atmospheric, low-crowd evening.

A modernista concert hall of stained glass, mosaic pillars and an inverted glass-dome skylight that floods the auditorium with daylight — Domènech i Montaner at his most exuberant. Take the guided tour, but far better: book a concert (the guitar recitals are magical) to hear it as it was meant to be experienced.

venues.n: Recinte Modernista de Sant Pau (Hospital de Sant Pau)
venues.d: The world's largest art nouveau site — a garden campus of mosaic-domed pavilions built as a hospital, now beautifully restored and refreshingly crowd-free. A short walk from the Sagrada Família and a serene counterpoint to it.

Set across five linked medieval palaces on Carrer Montcada, this holds the world's richest collection of Picasso's formative years — the classical training, the aching Blue Period, and his complete riff on Velázquez's 'Las Meninas.' Reserve ahead; the mansions themselves are half the pleasure.

Housed in the palatial Palau Nacional above the Magic Fountain, MNAC holds the finest collection of Romanesque church frescoes on earth — murals lifted whole from remote Pyrenean chapels. The rooftop terrace has one of the best free-ish city panoramas.

A luminous white building by Josep Lluís Sert, purpose-built to hold Miró's stars, symbols and sculptures with daylight and air. The sculpture roof-terrace and the calm hilltop setting make it the most restful of the big museums.

The soaring Gothic cathedral of Santa Eulàlia, with a cloister where thirteen white geese are kept (one for each year of the child-martyr's life). Take the lift to the roof for a close view over the medieval rooftops. Dress modestly to enter.

venues.n: Basílica de Santa Maria del Mar
venues.d: The purest Catalan Gothic in the city — the 'cathedral of the sea,' raised in the 14th century by the port stevedores who hauled the stones themselves. The interior is austere and breathtaking; sit for the sublime acoustics or catch an evening concert.

The medieval heart of Barcelona — a maze of narrow lanes, hidden plazas and Roman wall fragments. Wander without a map: find Plaça Sant Felip Neri with its shrapnel-scarred church, the Pont del Bisbe bridge, and cafés on Plaça Reial. Best early morning or late evening when the day-trippers thin out.

Barcelona's most stylish old quarter — designer boutiques, wine bars and craft ateliers threaded through medieval streets around Santa Maria del Mar. The Passeig del Born and Carrer Montcada are the spine; graze the tapas bars and independent shops at your own pace.

A former village that kept its own rhythm — leafy squares (Plaça del Sol, Plaça de la Vila) ringed by terrace cafés, independent designers and vermouth bars. The least touristy place to feel local Barcelona; time a visit to the wild Festa Major street-decoration festival in August.

The famous tree-lined promenade running from Plaça de Catalunya to the sea — flower stalls, the Boqueria market, and the mosaic by Miró underfoot at Pla de l'Os. Best walked briskly as a spine to the old town; keep valuables close, as it's pickpocket territory.

Barcelona's grand food cathedral — 300-plus stalls of jamón, seafood, fruit and jewel-bright juices under a modernista iron roof. Skip the entrance crush and go deep to the back where locals eat; the counter stools at Bar Pinotxo are an institution. Go before 10am for the calm, quality version.

A working neighbourhood market under an undulating, candy-coloured mosaic roof by architect Enric Miralles. Far less touristed than the Boqueria — come for cheese, olives and a quiet counter lunch where locals actually shop.

Barcelona's grandest avenue and its luxury-shopping spine — flagship maisons (Louis Vuitton, Chanel, Loewe) housed beneath the modernista facades of the 'Block of Discord,' where Casa Batlló and Casa Amatller sit side by side. The one address that rewards a discerning, unhurried afternoon.

venues.n: Bunkers del Carmel (Turó de la Rovira)
venues.d: A former Civil War anti-aircraft battery on a 262m hilltop with a full 360-degree sweep over the whole city to the sea. The locals' sunset spot — bring a bottle and a jacket. Free, but a proper climb; a taxi or private car to the base saves the legs.

Barcelona's highest point at 512m, crowned by the neo-Gothic Sagrat Cor church (take the lift to the roof) and a charming century-old amusement park with a Ferris wheel over the whole coastline. On a clear day you can see the Pyrenees. A great multi-generation half-day.

The green hill above the port, laced with gardens, museums and Olympic venues. Ride the Telefèric de Montjuïc up to the 17th-century castle for harbour views, then wander down through the terraced gardens. A relaxed, uncrowded half-day away from the old-town bustle.

A grand 1929 fountain that performs a free choreographed show of water, light and music below the illuminated Palau Nacional. An easy, crowd-pleasing evening for families — check the seasonal schedule, as shows run only certain nights.

The city's oldest and greenest public park, built for the 1888 World's Fair — a monumental cascade fountain (young Gaudí had a hand in it), a rowing lake, and shaded lawns. The nearest thing to a picnic-and-slow-down morning in central Barcelona; the zoo and parliament sit within it.

The city beach — a broad crescent of sand backed by seafood terraces and the long Passeig Marítim promenade. Walk it at golden hour, hire a paddleboard, or book a private day sail out of Port Vell. For a calmer swim, the northern beaches (Bogatell, Nova Icària) are cleaner and quieter.

The revamped old harbour — superyacht marina, the Rambla de Mar footbridge, and the aquarium's shark tunnel for younger travellers. A pleasant stroll linking the Gothic Quarter to the beach; the marina is where private charters and sunset cruises depart.

Gaudí's early, darker masterpiece — a six-storey city palace for his patron Eusebi Güell, built around a soaring parabolic-domed central hall pierced with starlight-like holes, and a roof of technicolour trencadís chimneys. Quiet and often overlooked, just off La Rambla.

Gaudí's very first house, a riot of green-and-white tiles, ironwork and Moorish motifs that shows the young genius already breaking every rule. Recently opened to the public and rarely crowded — the connoisseur's Gaudí stop.

venues.a: Santa Coloma de Cervelló (edge of Barcelona)
venues.d: A short train ride out of the city to Gaudí's astonishing brick-and-basalt crypt — the structural laboratory where he tested the leaning columns and catenary arches later used in the Sagrada Família. Set in a preserved modernista workers' village; peaceful and uncrowded.

Barcelona's opera house since 1847 and one of the world's great lyric theatres, its gilded horseshoe auditorium rebuilt after a 1994 fire. Book a box for an opera or a recital, or take the guided tour of the mirror hall — the grand cultural evening in the city.

Richard Meier's luminous white building anchoring gritty-cool El Raval, with a strong post-war and contemporary collection. The sloping plaza out front is Europe's most famous skateboarding spot — a bit of living street culture that pairs with the art inside.

The city's sharpest ideas venue — ambitious exhibitions on cities, technology and culture, film seasons and talks, set in a restored former almshouse next to MACBA. Where thoughtful travellers go to take Barcelona's intellectual pulse.

Barcelona's most multicultural and fast-changing quarter — vintage shops on Carrer de la Riera Baixa, Rodríguez's fat cat sculpture on the Rambla del Raval, and a wave of new galleries and design bars. Edgy and characterful; wander in daylight and stay on the busier streets at night.

A former industrial district reborn as Barcelona's creative-tech quarter — the leafy Rambla del Poblenou, converted-factory galleries, and quieter beaches (Bogatell) just beyond. Monthly design and vintage markets; a low-key, local counterpoint to the old town.

A neighbourhood at the foot of Montjuïc built around a pedestrian pintxo strip — bar after bar of Basque-style skewers at a euro or two apiece, plus Albert Adrià's acclaimed Bodega 1900 nearby. The relaxed, delicious local answer to a big dinner out.

One of Europe's oldest flea markets, reborn under a spectacular mirrored-canopy roof — 300-plus stalls of antiques, vintage, curios and genuine treasure among the junk. Come with time and patience; the mornings (Mon/Wed/Fri/Sat) are best.

A beautifully restored 19th-century iron market hall — everyday food shopping mid-week, and a beloved Sunday book, comic and collectors' market spilling around the outside. The surrounding streets have become one of the city's best low-key food-and-drink zones.

One of Europe's finest science museums, best known for its 'Flooded Forest' — a full glasshouse slice of Amazon rainforest with live piranhas and crocodiles — and a towering geological wall of real rock. Superb, hands-on, and genuinely engaging for children and adults alike.

Barcelona's oldest garden (1791) — a neoclassical estate with a romantic hedge maze, cypress avenues, pavilions and a still lake, capped at 750 visitors at a time so it stays serene. A hidden, aristocratic retreat far from the tourist trail; magical with children.

An open-air 'Spanish village' of 117 buildings replicating architecture from every region, built for the 1929 Expo — plus artisan workshops, galleries and glassblowers at work. Touristy but genuinely fun for families; a painless way to sample all of Spain in an afternoon.

FC Barcelona's colossal stadium, one of Europe's largest, freshly rebuilt and reopened. The immersive museum-and-pitch tour is a pilgrimage for football-mad families; match tickets, when the season's on, are the electric option.

An intimate flamenco tablao inside a candlelit Baroque palace on Carrer Montcada — a single guitarist, singer and dancer at close range rather than a big touristy revue. The atmospheric way to experience the art form; book the early evening seating.

A Benedictine monastery dramatically wedged into a jagged, saw-toothed massif, home to the revered 'Black Madonna' (La Moreneta) and the Escolania boys' choir, which sings most days. Ride the rack railway or cable car up, then walk the ridge trails. A private car and guide make it an effortless half-day of nature and pilgrimage.

venues.a: Day trip (~40 min by high-speed train)
venues.d: A jewel-box medieval city — a magnificent Gothic cathedral with the widest nave in the world, one of Europe's best-preserved Jewish quarters (El Call), and the pastel houses of the Onyar river (a 'Game of Thrones' backdrop). Nearby El Celler de Can Roca is one of the world's top restaurants; book far ahead.

An elegant seaside town of white villas, modernista mansions and golden beaches, long a bohemian and artists' haunt. Stroll the promenade to the church on its headland, lunch on the seafront, and dip in the Mediterranean. The easy, glamorous coastal escape from the city.
The best bar in the world in 2023, and Europe's best three years running — Simone Caporale and Marc Álvarez's cutting-edge cocktail counter.
A speakeasy behind the fridge door of a pastrami shop — a whale-ribbed room and some of the most theatrical drinks anywhere.
An apothecary of a bar — ferments, distillates and house ingredients lining the walls, from the Paradiso team.
Barcelona's oldest cocktail bar, open since 1933 — a tiny, standing-room Art Deco room where the drinks are shaken, not poured.
A confident new arrival on the world list — inventive, produce-led drinks in an easy, modern room.
A self-styled 'five-star dive bar' on a Raval side street — irreverent, warm, and seriously good at cocktails.
The old bank vault of the Mandarin Oriental turned intimate cocktail bar — polished, discreet, and expertly made.
The Mandarin Oriental's rooftop terrace and dipping pool — a considered drink above Passeig de Gràcia.
